questions.q: A tannoy repeats every announcement four times. Write a program that prints a message four times.
brief: Read one word - the message.
Print it four times, one on each line.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read the message, then print it four times

tests.why: Four lines exactly. Five lines means range(5) - range(4) already gives four turns, counting 0, 1, 2, 3.
The message is read from the user, so a program with the word typed into it will fail here.
A one letter message is still repeated four times.

questions.fb: range(4) counts 0, 1, 2, 3 - four numbers, so the loop body runs four times even though it never reaches 4.

questions.q: Write a program that repeats a word as many times as the user asks for.
brief: Read one word on the first line.
Read one whole number on the second line - how many times to repeat it.
Print: start
Then print the word that many times, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Read a word and a count, print start, then repeat the word

tests.why: 'start' is printed once, before the loop, so it must not be inside it.
A count of 1 means one repeat. Two lines of 'tap' means you looped to n + 1.
range(0) runs no turns at all, so only 'start' is printed. A line of 'hum' here means your loop always runs at least once.
The number has to come from input(), and remember int() - range() cannot use the text '5'.

questions.fb: range(n) uses whatever number is in n, including 0, which simply means the body never runs.

questions.q: Write a program that numbers the lanes of a swimming pool.
brief: Read one whole number - how many lanes there are.
Print the lane numbers from 1 up to and including that number, one on each line.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read how many lanes there are, then number them from 1

tests.why: Starts at 1 and includes 5. A list starting at 0 means you used range(n) instead of range(1, n + 1).
One lane gives one line. Nothing printed at all means range(1, n) stopped before it started.
The last number must appear. Missing 3 is the off by one that range(1, n) always causes.

questions.fb: range stops before its second number, so to finish on n you have to write range(1, n + 1).

questions.q: A tiler needs the area of each square slab from 1 metre upwards. Write a program that lists them.
brief: Read one whole number - the largest side length in metres.
For every side length from 1 up to and including that number, print one line:
the side length, a single space, then that side length multiplied by itself.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read the largest side, then print each side and its area

tests.why: The counter is used twice on each line - once on its own and once multiplied by itself.
A side of 1 has an area of 1, so the two numbers on the line are the same here.
Every line must use its own counter value. Lines that all show the same number mean you are printing n rather than i.
Two lines only. A third line means your range went one too far.

questions.fb: The loop variable is an ordinary number, so you can calculate with it inside the loop - i * i changes on every turn.

questions.q: A school hall has numbered rows. Write a program that lists the rows in a block from a first row to a last row.
brief: Read two whole numbers, one on each line - the first row number, then the last row number.
Print every row number from the first up to and including the last, one on each line.
The last row number will never be smaller than the first.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read the first and last row numbers, then list every row in between

tests.why: Both ends are included. A missing 7 means you wrote range(first, last).
The first and last row are the same, so exactly one line is printed. Nothing at all means your range was empty.
The start has to come from the input. A list beginning at 0 or 1 means you ignored the first number.
Four lines. Five means you added 1 to the start as well as the end.

questions.fb: range takes a start and a stop, and the stop is never reached, so include the last value by writing last + 1.

questions.q: A gauge is read five times, going up or down by a fixed amount each time. Write a program that prints the five readings.
brief: Read two whole numbers, one on each line - the first reading, then the step.
Print five readings, one on each line, starting at the first reading and changing by the step each time.
The step may be negative, in which case the readings count down.
The step will never be 0.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read the first reading and the step, then print five readings

tests.why: Five readings, starting at the first one. Starting at 7 means you added the step before printing instead of after.
A negative step counts down. Nothing printed means your range still goes upwards - the third number in range has to be negative too.
A step of 1 is the ordinary case, and there must still be exactly five lines.
Counting down can pass through 0, so do not stop the loop early when the reading gets small.
A negative start with a positive step. The start is just a number - there is nothing special to do about the minus sign.

questions.fb: range takes a third number, the step: range(start, stop, step). A negative step counts down, and the stop still has to be past the last value you want.

questions.q: A tuck shop counts up the day's takings. Write a program that totals a set of amounts.
brief: Read one whole number - how many amounts follow.
Then read that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Print only the total of those amounts.
questions.starter: # Read how many amounts there are, add them up, print the total

tests.why: The total starts at 0 and grows on every turn of the loop.
One amount. If you got 0 you printed the total before the loop had added anything.
A refund is negative, so use total = total + amount rather than only adding when the amount is large.
Two zeros total 0, and that single line still has to be printed.
The loop must run exactly as many times as the first number says, and only the total is printed - not each amount.

questions.fb: A running total needs three things: set it to 0 before the loop, add to it inside the loop, print it after the loop.

questions.q: A weather club logs the overnight temperature for a week. Write a program that reports on the readings.
brief: Read one whole number - how many readings follow.
Then read that many whole numbers, one on each line - temperatures in degrees Celsius.
Print four lines, in this order:
Line 1: the total of all the readings.
Line 2: how many readings are below 0.
Line 3: the highest reading.
Line 4: the lowest reading.
questions.starter: # Read the readings, then print the total, the frosty count, the highest and the lowest

tests.why: One reading is below 0, and the highest and lowest are both in the list - neither is a number you invented.
Every reading is negative, so a highest that starts at 0 will wrongly stay 0. Start it at the first reading instead.
With one reading it is both the highest and the lowest, and nothing is below 0.
Exactly 0 is not below 0, so the count stays at 0 - this is where < and <= get mixed up.
The highest value appears twice, which must not be counted twice in the total or change the answer.

questions.fb: Keep a separate variable for each thing you are tracking, and update them all inside the same loop. For a highest or lowest, start from the first reading, not from 0.

questions.q: Write a program that draws a rectangle of stars of any size.
brief: Read two whole numbers, one on each line - the number of rows, then the number of stars in each row.
Print the rectangle: one line per row, each line made of that many * characters with nothing between them.
Print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read the rows and the width, then draw the rectangle of stars

tests.why: Three rows of four stars. A single line of twelve stars means your print is inside the inner loop.
The smallest rectangle is one star. Nothing printed means a range that never runs.
The rows and the width are different numbers, so check you have not swapped them.
More rows than stars per row. If you got two rows of four stars, the two inputs are the wrong way round.

questions.fb: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop builds one row. Build the row into a string first, then print it once the inner loop has finished.

questions.q: Write a program that prints a multiplication square.
brief: Read one whole number - the size of the square.
Print that many lines. The line for row r holds r times 1, r times 2, and so on up to r times the size.
Put a single space between the numbers on a line.
For a size of 3 the output is exactly these three lines: 1 2 3 then 2 4 6 then 3 6 9.
questions.starter: # Read the size, then print the multiplication square

tests.why: Both loops run from 1, not 0 - a square full of zeros on the first row means one of them started at 0.
A size of 1 gives one line holding 1 times 1.
Four lines of four numbers. Three lines means both ranges needed n + 1.
The row number is fixed while the inner loop runs, so the outer counter must be used in the multiplication too.

questions.fb: The outer counter stays still while the inner one runs all the way through, and the number you print is the two counters multiplied together.

questions.q: A spelling game scores words by how many vowels they hold. Write a program that reports on a set of words.
brief: Read one whole number - how many words follow.
Then read that many words, one on each line, all in lower case.
For each word, print one line: the word, a single space, then how many vowels it holds.
After all the words, print one more line: the total number of vowels in all of them.
The vowels are a, e, i, o and u.
questions.starter: # Read the words, print each one with its vowel count, then the grand total

tests.why: Each word gets its own line and its own count, and the last line is the two counts added together.
A word with no vowels still prints a line, with 0. A missing line means you only print when a vowel is found.
The count has to be reset to 0 for each word, inside the outer loop. Counts that keep growing mean you set it to 0 only once, before the loop.
All five vowels counted, and the total ignores the word with none.
The same vowel twice counts twice, so go through the letters one at a time rather than checking whether a letter is present.

questions.fb: Two counters do different jobs here: one resets for each word, inside the outer loop, and the total is set up once before it and printed once after it.
